newsitem.title: INDIA: India cautious over U.S. rights assessment.
newsitem.headline: India cautious over U.S. rights assessment.

text.p: Criticism by the United States of India's human rights record drew a cautious response on Friday from Indian officials who discerned an improvement in Washington's stand but questioned its right to assess India.

Indian officials and analysts frowned on Washington's right to slam human rights violations in India, but the U.S. State Department's mention that separatist militants were also violating human rights in India drew a positive response.

The State Department said in its annual human rights report released on Thursday that in India, there continued to be "significant human rights abuses, despite constitutional and statutory safeguards."

"Compared to two three years ago at least there is a recognition that militants are at the root of the substantivie problem which was not there earlier," said Jasjit Singh, director of the state-funded Institute for Defence Studies and Analysis. "There is a definite change in attitude."
He said the United States had for long refused to acknowledge foreign aid to Indian separatists in the Himalayan Kashmir region.

Singh did not name any country, but was referring to a frequent charge by India that Pakistan aids Moslem rebels in the region it disputes. "By keeping one eye closed they (the United States) only prolonged the agony," he said.
Pakistan, which has fought two wars with India over Kashmir, denies Indian charges it arms the separatists, who launched in 1990 a rebellion which has resulted in more than 20,000 deaths.
Indian Foreign Ministry spokesmen could not be reached for comment.

Former diplomat Brijesh Mishra, now a foreign policy expert for the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), said the State Department should not analyse human rights records in the first place.
"It is not a good practice for any country to bring out reports of this kind on human rights in another country. If at all, it should be in the United Nations," Mishra said.
"This is from a country which has taken upon itself the task of human rights as if it is supranational," Mishra said.
